summary: God speaks from Sinai, first identifying himself as the one who brought Israel out of bondage, then giving commands concerning worship, the divine name, Sabbath, parents, and neighbors. The people tremble at the storm and ask Moses to mediate, after which Yahweh forbids metal gods alongside him and gives instructions for simple altars of earth or uncut stone.
whyItMatters: The foundational commands are introduced by rescue and address household rest as well as worship and harm to neighbors. The terrified response and altar instructions keep the public voice and the worship setting attached to the words.

context.author: Exodus names no writer of the finished book, though it depicts Moses writing particular words. Later tradition ascribes the Torah to him; its composition remains debated.
context.audience: Israel is addressed through its story of rescue, covenant, and worship; this chapter names no narrower first audience.
context.date: The book gives a relative story sequence but no secure external year for the events. The dating and formation of its finished text remain debated.
context.setting: Mount Sinai and the people standing at a distance, followed by instructions for altars wherever Yahweh records his name.
context.literaryForm: Divine covenant speech, a brief mediation scene, and altar regulations.

before.text: Israel has accepted the covenant proposal and prepared within marked bounds while Yahweh descends in fire and cloud. God’s speech now begins from that mountain scene.

here.text: Commands move from exclusive worship to family and neighbor obligations; the people recoil from the voice and receive directions for worship without rival images.

after.text: The following chapter begins detailed case laws with rules concerning Hebrew servants, violence, injury, and household responsibility.

outline.heading: Rescue and exclusive worship
outline.note: God identifies the deliverance from bondage and forbids other gods and images.

outline.heading: Name and Sabbath
outline.note: Misuse of Yahweh’s name is prohibited, and seventh-day rest includes household members and animals.

outline.heading: Parents and neighbors
outline.note: Honor, murder, adultery, theft, false testimony, and coveting are addressed.

outline.heading: The people fear the direct voice
outline.note: They stand back and ask Moses to speak with them while he approaches the darkness.

outline.heading: No metal gods; simple altars
outline.note: Yahweh forbids rival silver and gold images and specifies earth or uncut-stone altars.

keyVerses.text: “I am Yahweh your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage.
keyVerses.why: The commands begin by identifying Yahweh as the one who brought Israel out of bondage.

keyVerses.text: but the seventh day is a Sabbath to Yahweh your God. You shall not do any work in it, you, nor your son, nor your daughter, your male servant, nor your female servant, nor your livestock, nor your stranger who is within your gates;
keyVerses.why: Sabbath rest explicitly reaches children, servants, livestock, and resident strangers.

keyVerses.text: They said to Moses, “Speak with us yourself, and we will listen; but don’t let God speak with us, lest we die.”
keyVerses.why: The people’s request for Moses to mediate follows their fear of hearing God directly.

questions.question: Why does the speech begin with Egypt before any prohibition?
questions.answer: God first identifies himself as the one who brought Israel out of the land of Egypt and the house of bondage. The commands are presented to a rescued people within that ongoing covenant encounter.

questions.question: What is an “idol” in the first commands?
questions.answer: It is an image made to represent a god and receive bowing or service, with examples drawn from sky, earth, and water. The speech joins the image ban to the demand for exclusive worship of Yahweh.

questions.question: Does the line about children and parents authorize punishing children for a parent’s wrongdoing?
questions.answer: The speech says Yahweh visits ancestral iniquity to later generations “of those who hate me” and contrasts this with loving kindness to thousands who love him. It is a difficult claim about divine judgment, not a command for people to punish a child for a parent’s act.

questions.question: What is misuse of Yahweh’s name in this command?
questions.answer: The text forbids taking or using Yahweh’s name wrongly and warns that such misuse is not guiltless. It gives a broad prohibition but no list of cases in this verse.

questions.question: Who receives Sabbath rest?
questions.answer: The command includes the addressed adult, children, male and female servants, livestock, and the resident stranger. It grounds the seventh-day pattern in the creation account, giving rest a scope wider than the household head alone.

questions.question: How does “You shall not murder” relate to the book’s battle scenes?
questions.answer: This command prohibits murder, while the narrative has already described the battle at the sea and at Rephidim. The verse itself does not define every distinction among killing, warfare, and legal judgment, so those scenes cannot be used to erase the prohibition.

questions.question: What is the difference between theft and coveting in the list?
questions.answer: The command against stealing addresses taking what belongs to another, while the coveting line names desire directed toward a neighbor’s house, spouse, servants, animals, or property. The final command reaches an intention before any taking occurs.

questions.question: Why do the people keep their distance after hearing God?
questions.answer: They perceive thunder, lightning, trumpet sound, and smoke and fear that direct speech will kill them. Moses says God has come to test them and prevent sin, while he approaches the thick darkness as their mediator.

questions.question: Why do altar instructions follow the commands?
questions.answer: Yahweh says the people have heard him speak from heaven and again forbids silver or gold gods alongside him. He then specifies earth or uncut-stone altars for offerings, keeping worship practices tied to the encounter rather than detached from it.

glossary.def: The seventh day set apart for rest by the whole household, including servants, animals, and resident strangers.
To desire what the final command lists in another household, including a spouse, servants, animals, and goods.
The place prescribed for offerings, here made of earth or uncut stone rather than carved blocks.
